newsitem.title: GERMANY: German carmakers get fresh fuel from higher dollar.
newsitem.headline: German carmakers get fresh fuel from higher dollar.

text.p: German carmaker shares, particularly Volkswagen AG, are getting fresh fuel to keep up their unprecedented advance as analysts said on Tuesday the sector will stay among the best European performers.
Volkswagen shares, which ended bourse trade on Tuesday at 1,467 marks, have risen an astounding 130 percent so far in 1997, while the 30-share DAX has risen a mere 40 percent.

The Wolfsburg-based company, along with BMW AG and Porsche AG, are top favourites to keep up their sharp advances because their growing export-driven business makes their products cheaper abroad due to the stronger dollar.
German cars are also back in vogue. VW is profiting from a product offensive ranging from the compact Polo to the new Audi A8 and BMW is seeing strong demand.

Porsche has added more capacity to meet demand for its popular two-seater Boxster, a move that prompted Lehman Brothers analyst Chris Will this month to raise his price target on Porsche by 20 percent to 3,600 marks.

Another factor pushing VW higher is expected strong demand for the new Golf model, to be unveiled this autumn at the Frankfurt car show, and cost-cutting measures implemented by Ferdinand Piech that are starting to show their fruits.
"We are still very positive on VW and BMW," said Stephen Reitman, automotive analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.

"VW is certainly our favourite stock across Europe in terms of earnings growth potential and the visibility of the earnings stream into the year 2000. The objectives that management have set out appear to be attainable, namely a 6.5 percent to eight percent pre-tax return on sales," Reitman said.
The focus is not only on the dollar to help justify the gains. The rising pound is another positive factor because the region is another top export market for German carmakers.

"The dollar and sterling are both very positive influences. The German industry is the only part of the European motor industry that has a double positive in exchange rates, since they are the only major exporters in the U.S. and also to the U.K," said John Lawson, analyst at Salomon Brothers.
"This is a double whammy which is very positive," he said.
The surge in German carmakerS' shares has broken many price targets among industry analysts but has not brought out any warnings of a pending correction or for interest to fade.

Instead, many analysts said investors will stay in the industry sector, particularly VW for its dramatic turnaround after a massive 1.9 billion mark net loss in 1993 and also its unique position of making money in a dull European car market.

"They have the brand name, they are getting the costs down and are going for it," Sabine Bluemel, an automotive industry analyst at IMI Sigeco in London, said of Volkswagen. "This is what a lot of the other Europeans don't have."

Bluemel, who predicted VW shares could reach 1,650 marks, said VW remains the most undervalued in the sector given future earnings growth, trading on a 28 percent discount to the European sector and a 32 percent to the other European companies.
"The weightings are a bit heady," she said. "But as long as the DAX performs, it is a stock based on a good restructuring story and earnings potential. You get it all in one package."
BMW also rates a buy recommendation from many analysts, including Bluemel, since the share has been only performing on par with the DAX with a rise of 45 percent since January.
Some analysts said BMW has been weighed down by the strong pound and a perception among investors that BMW's share of profits will be wiped out by foreign exchange markets.

The opposite may be the case, analysts said, noting that BMW officials said last week at an analyst meeting in Britain that they would be worried only if sterling remains so strong for at least two years due to aggressive hedging programmes.

"You have to remember that BMW sells over 60,000 cars in the U.K. every year, so what is a drag for Rover is positive for another part of the group. In the end, by the time BMW and Rover become exposed, I would expect we would already see a much lower sterling rate anyway," Merrill's Reitman said.
